what: A common Āgamic scriptural and ritual form: scripture divided into four quarters (knowledge, yoga, ritual, conduct); graded initiations; mantra installation (nyāsa) and purification of the elements; the fire offering, image consecration and temple festival manuals.

evidence.detail: Both corpora divide scripture into four pādas (jñāna, yoga, kriyā, caryā) — the Śaiva Āgamas and Pāñcarātra saṃhitās such as the Pādma.
dīkṣā, nyāsa, bhūtaśuddhi, homa, pratiṣṭhā, utsava, maṇḍala.
Some historians hold that the early Pāñcarātra saṃhitās (Jayākhya, Sātvata, Pauṣkara) modelled their ritual on the Śaiva Mantramārga; others see a common Āgamic pool. Direction not settled.

The Pāñcarātra holds its saṃhitās to be spoken by Nārāyaṇa himself and authoritative in their own right (the 'three gems'); Yāmuna defends their Vedic authority. The Śaiva exegetes in turn rank the Pāñcarātrikas below themselves (they 'rest in the unmanifest'). Each tradition denies deriving from the other.

notes: New in U49 (no existing Śaiva Siddhānta↔Pāñcarātra entry). The Lakṣmī Tantra's Śaiva-like theology is recorded separately as brw:kashmir-saivism-to-laksmi-tantra (U23/U08).

what: The vocabulary and forms of Vedic ritual — fire offering (homa into a kuṇḍa with svāhā), consecration (dīkṣā) and royal anointing (abhiṣeka) — reused across the tantric families with new meanings (initiation into a mantra-lineage; consecration of the disciple as a 'king' of the maṇḍala).

evidence.detail: homa, kuṇḍa, āhuti, svāhā, dīkṣā, abhiṣeka recur in Śaiva, Pāñcarātra, Buddhist (homa rites; the crown and vajra consecrations) and Jain consecration manuals.
Historians trace the tantric abhiṣeka to the royal consecration and the tantric homa to the Vedic fire cult; the extent of dependence is debated.

The tantric families present their rites as a higher revelation: the Śaiva scriptures rank the Veda as the lower path; the Buddhist tantras distinguish their inner and outer fire offerings from the brahmins' sacrifice; Saraha mocks the brahmins' fire offering that only hurts their eyes with smoke.

notes: New in U49.

what: Tantric worship — initiation, nyāsa, maṇḍala and yantra, mantra-japa and temple consecration — taken into the later Purāṇas (the Agni Purāṇa's ritual chapters; the Śākta and Vaiṣṇava upapurāṇas).

evidence.detail: The Agni Purāṇa contains long manuals of dīkṣā, pratiṣṭhā and maṇḍala-worship parallel to Śaiva and Pāñcarātra paddhatis (recalled at chapter level).
The Purāṇas present these rites as their own teaching (Agni to Vasiṣṭha), not as borrowed from the tantras.
Dependence of parts of the Agni Purāṇa on Śaiva manuals such as the Somaśambhupaddhati has been proposed; not verified here.

notes: New in U49; chapter-level, to be checked in Phase C.

what: Mantra-kalpa ritual — seed syllables such as hrīṃ, yantras, body protection, the six rites for worldly ends, and the worship of goddesses such as Padmāvatī and Jvālāmālinī — within Jain practice.

evidence.detail: The Jain rite of 'sakalīkaraṇa' (protecting the body by placing mantras on the limbs) shares its name with the Śaiva preliminary nyāsa; the six rites (pacifying, attracting, subjugating, immobilising, driving away, killing) are the same list as in Śaiva/Śākta mantra manuals.
The Bhairava-Padmāvatī-kalpa requires devotion to the Jina and to the teacher as the qualification for its mantras — the rites are placed under Jain devotion.

notes: U49 addition: shared ritual vocabulary (sakalīkaraṇa, ṣaṭkarma) and the Jain framing of the rites.

what: The goddess Tārā (with Ekajaṭā and Akṣobhya) and the 'Cīna' mode of her worship

evidence.detail: On the Buddhist side the Sādhanamālā preserves sādhanas of Mahācīna-Tārā and Ekajaṭā; the Ekajaṭā practice is said there to have been brought back from Bhoṭa (Tibet) by Nāgārjuna (recalled; low confidence).

Buddhist Tārā is attested in images and hymns before the Hindu Tārā texts; scholars therefore usually take the Hindu Tārā of the Mahāvidyās to derive from the Buddhist goddess, as the Hindu texts' own Mahācīna story also implies.

notes: U49 addition: the Buddhist-side attestation and the scholarly account of priority; see cpt:tara-across-families.

what: Shared siddha names and songs (Mīna/Matsyendra, Jālandhara, Kāṇha, Cauraṅgī, Virūpa, Carpaṭi) and the eighty-four-siddha frame

evidence.detail: The fish-belly story is told of Mīnapa in the Buddhist Lives (Mīnapa overhears Śiva teaching Umā inside a fish) and of Matsyendra/Bhairava in the Kaulajñānanirṇaya (the scripture swallowed by a fish and recovered).
The Buddhist list makes Gorakṣa the cowherd who served the maimed Cauraṅgī — the same pair central to Nāth legend.
The Tibetan tradition ascribes the Amṛtasiddhi to Virūpa (Derge colophon); the Haṭhapradīpikā names Virūpākṣa among its mahāsiddhas.
A Maithili list of eighty-four siddhas (Varṇaratnākara) mixes Nāth and Buddhist names (recalled).

notes: U49 addition: the fish legend, the Gorakṣa–Cauraṅgī pair, the Virūpa attribution and the Varṇaratnākara list; the two lists are compared in cpt:eighty-four-siddhas-two-lists and cpt:siddha-identifications.

what: The rāga-set song signed by the siddha-poet (caryā; Nāth pad and sabad), the riddling images of the body, and the Old Bengali and Hindi milieu shared by the Buddhist Caryāgīti and the Nāth song-cycles (Gopīcandra, Mayanāmatī, Gorakh Bānī).

evidence.detail: Both use paradox and coded speech for the yoga of the body (the upside-down well, the tree of the body, the outcaste woman beyond the city).
Kāṇha signs Caryāgīti songs as a Buddhist siddha, while the Bengali Nāth cycles make Kānupā/Kānipā the disciple of Hāḍipā (Jālandhara) — the same master–disciple pair.
Historians of Bengali literature treat the Caryāpada and the Nāth songs as neighbouring strata of one regional siddha culture; the direction of influence is not established.

notes: New in U49.

what: The earliest haṭha doctrine and methods — bindu as the moon and essence of life, its consumption by the sun, the central channel, mahāmudrā/mahābandha/mahāvedha and the four stages — first appear in the Amṛtasiddhi, composed in a Buddhist tantric milieu.

evidence.detail: The Tibetan translation in the Derge Tengyur (Tōh 2285, among the siddhas' works) opens with homage to Śrī Heruka and closes: 'the Amṛtasiddhi composed by the great master Virūpa is complete' (read locally).
'mahāmudrā' names the bodily seal in the Amṛtasiddhi corpus and the haṭha texts but the ultimate realization in the Buddhist siddha literature — one word, two referents.

notes: U49 addition: the locally read Derge colophon and homage (explicit evidence of the Buddhist transmission), and the shifted sense of mahāmudrā. The haṭha tradition's own account (Ādinātha as source; HYP 1.1) is recorded in dsp:source-of-hatha-yoga.

what: The graded series of 'voids' — śūnya, atiśūnya, mahāśūnya — reached as knots are pierced in the haṭha four stages, parallel to the Buddhist completion stage's four empties (śūnya, atiśūnya, mahāśūnya, sarvaśūnya).

evidence.detail: Pañcakrama 2.4 names the empty, very empty, great empty and all-empty; HYP 4.70–75 has bliss from the void, the very void (atiśūnya) and the great void (mahāśūnya) in the first three stages.
The shared series may have passed through the Buddhist-milieu Amṛtasiddhi, which first teaches the four stages; this is a hypothesis only.

In the Buddhist texts the empties are stages of the dissolution of winds and concepts into clear light; in the haṭha texts they are places the breath reaches with inner sounds; neither tradition refers to the other.

notes: New in U49 (terms read in the local HYP and Pañcakrama teachings).

what: The names vajrolī, sahajolī and amarolī and the doctrine that bindu must be retained and drawn upward (summary only; restricted practice).

evidence.detail: 'vajra' as a code word for the male organ and 'sahaja' as the innate are Buddhist tantric usages; the haṭha names vajrolī and sahajolī use the same words.
Some historians argue that bindu-retention practices entered haṭha from Buddhist tantric sexual yoga through the Amṛtasiddhi corpus; the evidence is indirect.
The haṭha texts present vajrolī as Śiva's teaching and warn that it is hard to obtain and not for everyone; the Buddhist sources give their own restrictions.

notes: Restricted material: no method is recorded, only the names and the hypothesis.

what: The four attitudes maitrī, karuṇā, muditā, upekṣā (YS 1.33), called 'the abodes (vihāra) of meditators' in YBh 4.10.
era: early centuries CE (YS/YBh) — older Buddhist attestation

evidence.detail: A Buddhist text itself reports that wanderers of other sects taught the same four immeasurables and the abandoning of the hindrances, the Buddha claiming only that they cannot say where each culminates (SN 46.54).
YS 1.33 assigns each attitude to a class of beings (happy, suffering, virtuous, non-virtuous), as the Jain Tattvārtha 7.11 does; the Pali formula pervades the directions without classes.

notes: U49 addition: SN 46.54 as the Buddhist tradition's own witness to a shared milieu, and the structural parallel with the Jain formula (see brw:jain-four-bhavanas-and-yoga, dsp:yoga-buddhism-shared-milieu).

what: Four attitudes each directed at a class of beings — friendliness, joy/gladness, compassion, and impartiality/equanimity — in the Jain Tattvārtha (7.11) and in YS 1.33.
era: early centuries CE (relative dating of TS and YS uncertain)

evidence.detail: TS 7.11: friendliness toward all beings, joy toward the more virtuous, compassion toward the afflicted, impartiality toward the unruly; YS 1.33: friendliness toward the happy, compassion toward the suffering, gladness toward the virtuous, equanimity toward the non-virtuous.
The object-class form common to the Jain and Yoga texts suggests a shared śramaṇa formula rather than direct borrowing from the Buddhist brahmavihāras; direction unknown.

notes: New in U49; complements brw:buddhism-yoga-four-attitudes (U10).

what: The four immeasurables (love, compassion, rejoicing, equanimity) and the abandoning of the five hindrances as practices also taught by non-Buddhist wanderers, and framed in the suttas as the way to companionship with Brahmā.

evidence.detail: SN 46.54: other wanderers say 'we too teach our disciples thus'; the Buddha answers that only a Tathāgata or his disciple can say how each liberation of mind culminates.
In DN 13 the brahmavihāras are taught as the path to union with Brahmā, answering brahmins in their own terms.
Some scholars take the brahmavihāras to be pre-Buddhist contemplative practices adopted and reinterpreted by the Buddha; others hold them Buddhist in origin and later shared.

notes: New in U49.

what: The five restraints — non-violence, truth, non-stealing, celibacy, non-possession — and their name 'great vow' (mahāvrata) when kept without limitation.
era: Jain canon (c. 3rd c. BCE onward) → YS (early centuries CE); Dharmasūtra renouncer vows in between

evidence.detail: TS 7.1–2 lists the five and calls them 'great' when kept in full; YS 2.30–31 lists the same five as yamas and calls them the great vow when unlimited by birth, place, time or occasion.
mahāvrata is the standard Jain term for the mendicant's five vows.
The five-vow list is also found for Brahmanical renouncers in the Dharmasūtras; scholars debate whether Yoga took it from the Jains or from a common renouncer code.

notes: New in U49. The Yoga tradition presents the yamas as its own first limb without reference to the Jains.

what: Engagement with Buddhist idealism: the Yoga Sūtra and its bhāṣya state and reject the view that the object is only a construction of cognition (YS 4.14–16).

evidence.detail: The bhāṣya on 4.14 sets out the idealist argument (no object without cognition, as in dreams) and rejects it; YS 4.15–16 argue that one thing is shared by many minds and does not depend on a single mind.
Later Yoga commentators identify the opponent as the Buddhist Vijñānavādin (recalled for Vācaspati).

notes: New in U49. An engagement (polemical link), not an adoption; it dates the Yoga text relative to Yogācāra and shows the Yoga tradition marking its difference from Buddhism.

what: Mahāyāna and Yogācāra terms in the fourth book of the Māṇḍūkya-kārikā: agrayāna, tāyin, the awakened (buddhāḥ) who proclaim non-origination, dharmas pure by nature and awakened from the beginning, lokottara, kalpita-saṃvṛti and paratantra, and origination taught provisionally to those who fear non-origination.
era: c. 6th c. CE (scholarly date of the Kārikā)

evidence.detail: Advaita reads 'buddha' as 'the wise', 'dharma' as the selves and 'agrayāna' as the foremost means, and takes GK 4.99 ('this was not spoken by the Buddha') to mark the Upaniṣadic non-dual self off from Buddhist teaching; Śaṅkara's commentary says the Buddhist mind-only doctrine comes close but the non-dual reality is known from the Upaniṣads alone.
Many modern scholars see the Alātaśānti as written in dialogue with (or under the influence of) Madhyamaka and Yogācāra; its degree of dependence is debated.

notes: New in U49: the vocabulary evidence is distinct from brw:madhyamaka-to-gaudapada (arguments, firebrand) and brw:yogacara-to-gaudapada (dream argument).

what: The argument that nothing arises from itself, another, both or neither; the firebrand-circle simile; the language of non-origination and of the pacification of elaboration in Gauḍapāda's Māṇḍūkya Kārikā, especially book 4 (Alātaśānti).
era: Madhyamaka c. 2nd–3rd c.; Gauḍapāda c. 6th c. CE (scholarly)

evidence.detail: Local GRETIL text: GK 4.22 (nothing is born from itself or another, as existent, non-existent or both) and 4.47–48 (consciousness vibrating like a firebrand).
Śaṅkara's commentary on GK 4.99 grants the closeness and denies the identity.

notes: U49 addition: verse-level refs from the local text and the Advaita commentary's denial.

what: The dialectic that refutes every definition offered by the opponent without committing to a thesis of one's own, and the conclusion that the world of difference is indeterminable (anirvacanīya).

evidence.detail: Śrīharṣa himself raises the charge that his method is the Mādhyamika's and answers that the two agree on the indeterminability of the world but the Brahma-vādin exempts self-luminous consciousness.
The Advaita tradition holds that the method serves the Upaniṣadic Brahman and denies any borrowing of doctrine.
Historians compare Śrīharṣa's method with Nāgārjuna's prasaṅga; similarity of method is widely accepted, dependence is debated.

notes: New in U49.

what: The distinction of a conventional (saṃvṛti/vyavahāra) and an ultimate (paramārtha) truth, and the use of 'saṃvṛti' in Gauḍapāda.

evidence.detail: GK 4.73–74 speaks of what exists by 'imagined convention' (kalpita-saṃvṛti) but not ultimately; MMK 24.8 grounds the teaching in the two truths.
Advaita derives its levels from the Upaniṣads — the higher and lower knowledge of the Muṇḍaka and the 'as if there were duality' of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka — and denies Buddhist dependence.
The two-truth vocabulary in Gauḍapāda is often cited as Buddhist influence; others note Upaniṣadic antecedents.

notes: New in U49; see cpt:levels-of-truth-across-families.

what: The Buddhist claim that what is acceptable in the Vedānta (non-duality, freedom from conceptual construction) is the Buddha's teaching of emptiness.

evidence.detail: Bhāviveka's chapter on the Vedānta answers the doctrine of the one self and grants its acceptable points only as the emptiness taught by the Buddha.
The Vedānta tradition rejects the claim: Śaṅkara refutes the Buddhist schools and calls the Buddha's teaching incoherent; GK 4.99 says the non-dual self 'was not spoken by the Buddha'.

notes: New in U49. Both sides are tradition accounts; no verdict is given.

what: The organization of renouncers into monastic centres (maṭha) with a lineage of abbots and regional seats.

evidence.detail: The Advaita tradition holds that Śaṅkara founded the four (or five) seats and the ten names of the Daśanāmī order, continuing Upaniṣadic renunciation.
Some historians suggest that the Advaita monastic institutions were modelled on the Buddhist saṅgha; the historical evidence for the early maṭhas is late and debated.

notes: New in U49; low confidence — a commonly repeated hypothesis, flagged for Phase C.

what: The epistemological framework and vocabulary of Dignāga's and Dharmakīrti's school - the particular and the conceptual, exclusion (apoha/apohana), self-awareness, causal efficacy - taken up by Utpaladeva and turned against the no-self thesis.

evidence.detail: Consciousness defined by reflexive awareness (svasaṃvedana/vimarśa) in ĪPK 1.5.13, turned from a Buddhist doctrine of momentary cognition into the Lord's self-awareness.
The Pratyabhijñā presents itself as answering the Buddhist logicians; the dispute is recorded as dsp:pratyabhijna-vs-buddhist-logicians.

notes: U49 addition: the reflexive-awareness evidence and the link to the dispute.

what: Theory of inference and debate: members of the demonstration, pseudo-reasons, and later the concept of pervasion, developed in mutual criticism

evidence.detail: Uddyotakara opens the Vārttika by saying he writes to remove the errors of 'bad reasoners' (kutārkika), whom the tradition identifies with Dignāga's school.

notes: U49 addition: Uddyotakara's own opening verse.

what: The framework of Buddhist logic — inference for oneself and for others, fallacies of thesis and reason — adopted and argued against in Jain logic (Nyāyāvatāra; Akalaṅka's replies to Dharmakīrti).

evidence.detail: Śāntarakṣita's examination of inference sets out and answers Pātrasvāmin's 'otherwise-impossibility' as the single mark of a reason — the Buddhist side of the same exchange.

notes: U49 addition: a teaching record for the Tattvasaṃgraha passage.

what: The Nyāya framework of means of knowledge (pratyakṣa, anumāna, āgama), the debate vocabulary and many definitions, adopted by Jain logicians and fitted to the canonical scheme of five knowledges.

evidence.detail: Siddhasena's Nyāyāvatāra, Akalaṅka and Hemacandra's Pramāṇamīmāṃsā use the Nyāya/Buddhist terms pramāṇa, pakṣa, hetu, dṛṣṭānta, hetvābhāsa, vāda.
The Jain tradition grounds its epistemology in the canon: the five knowledges (mati, śruta, avadhi, manaḥparyaya, kevala) are themselves the two means of knowledge, indirect and direct.
Jain logicians reject Nyāya's permission of wrangling (jalpa) and cavil (vitaṇḍā) and its Īśvara (Hemacandra's Anyayogavyavacchedikā with the Syādvādamañjarī).

notes: New in U49; complements brw:pramana-buddhist-to-jain-logic.

what: Mutual critique that shaped both epistemologies: intrinsic versus extrinsic validity of cognition, the authorless Veda and the impossibility of an omniscient teacher (Mīmāṃsā) against Buddhist apoha, momentariness and the omniscient Buddha.

evidence.detail: Kumārila's Ślokavārttika has a chapter refuting apoha; Śāntarakṣita's Tattvasaṃgraha has examinations answering Kumārila on the seer of supersensible things; Bhāviveka examines the Mīmāṃsā doctrine of the authorless Veda.
The shared formulation of the intrinsic/extrinsic validity question is seen as a product of this exchange.

notes: New in U49.

what: Debate between Sāṃkhya and Buddhist teachers in the 4th–5th c.: the Sāṃkhya teacher Vindhyavāsin and the Buddhist replies ascribed to Vasubandhu.

evidence.detail: Paramārtha's Chinese Life of Vasubandhu tells that Vindhyavāsin defeated Vasubandhu's teacher Buddhamitra in debate and that Vasubandhu answered with a treatise (the 'Paramārthasaptati', now lost) (recalled).
Historians connect Vindhyavāsin's revisions of Sāṃkhya with this exchange.

notes: New in U49; low confidence, recalled from the Chinese biography.

what: A Sāṃkhya-like teaching placed in the mouth of the bodhisattva's first teacher Arāḍa Kālāma: prakṛti (the five elements, I-maker, intellect, unmanifest) and its modifications, the field-knower, ignorance, action and craving as causes of saṃsāra, a five-jointed ignorance, and liberation of the field-knower as the supreme Brahman — rejected by the bodhisattva because a self remains.

evidence.detail: The five-jointed ignorance (tamas, moha, mahāmoha, tāmisra, andhatāmisra) has the same names as the five misconceptions of Sāṃkhyakārikā 47–48; eight prakṛtis and sixteen modifications resemble the epic Sāṃkhya of the Mokṣadharma.
Arāḍa names Kapila as the awakened one and Jaigīṣavya, Janaka and Parāśara as freed by his path.
In the Pali account (MN 26) Āḷāra Kālāma teaches the attainment of nothingness with no Sāṃkhya doctrine; the Sāṃkhya colouring is Aśvaghoṣa's presentation.
Scholars read canto 12 as a witness to a pre-classical, epic-period Sāṃkhya known to Buddhist authors.

notes: New in U49 (read in the local Buddhacarita). The formless attainments themselves are recorded as brw:formless-attainments-from-teachers (U36).

what: Jain engagement with Pātañjala yoga: Haribhadra's yoga works (Yogadṛṣṭisamuccaya, Yogabindu) correlate his eight views with the eight limbs; Hemacandra's Yogaśāstra adapts prāṇāyāma, pratyāhāra and dhāraṇā; Yaśovijaya wrote on selected sūtras.

evidence.detail: Hemacandra and Śubhacandra take up breath-control but judge it unnecessary for liberation and disturbing to the mind — the Jain qualification of the adopted yoga.
Haribhadra's eight views are correlated with the limbs beginning with yama.

notes: U49 addition: the Jain authors' own reservations about prāṇāyāma and the verse correlating the eight views with the limbs.

what: The fourfold scheme of meditation objects — the embodied (piṇḍastha), the word (padastha), the form (rūpastha) and the formless (rūpātīta) — found in Jain yoga manuals and in Śaiva/Kaula and Nāth sources.

evidence.detail: Hemacandra's Yogaśāstra 7.8 and Śubhacandra's Jñānārṇava name the four; the same four terms occur in Śaiva tantric (Kaula, Kubjikā) and Nāth texts on meditation (recalled; sources not located here).
Scholars take the Jain scheme to be adapted from Śaiva tantric sources, as with the five element-concentrations of embodied meditation.
The Jain texts fill the scheme with Jain content (the Arhat's form, the bodiless Siddha, the syllable arhaṃ).

notes: New in U49; the Śaiva/Nāth attestation is recalled, not located (flagged in REPORT.md). Related: brw:saiva-bhutasuddhi-to-jain-dharanas (U35).

what: The Kashmiri aesthetics of rasa as relish in the responsive subject and the acceptance of śānta as a rasa, behind the Gauḍīya theory of bhakti-rasa (with śānta as the first of five primary devotional rasas).

evidence.detail: Abhinava defends śānta rasa with knowledge of reality as its stable emotion; Rūpa builds bhakti-rasa from the same components (sthāyibhāva, vibhāva, anubhāva, sāttvika, vyabhicārin) and counts śānta among the primary devotional rasas.
The route may be indirect — through Mammaṭa's Kāvyaprakāśa, Viśvanātha's Sāhityadarpaṇa and Bhoja's Śṛṅgāraprakāśa (love as the root rasa), to which Rūpa is in some respects closer than to Abhinava.

The Gauḍīya tradition derives bhakti-rasa from the Bhāgavata ('drink the Bhāgavata, the abode of rasa') and holds that worldly rasa is not true rasa; it does not present its theory as taken from the poeticians.

notes: New in U49; complements brw:alankara-rasa-to-gaudiya (U16), which records the adoption of Bharata's categories from lin:alankara.

what: Śaiva ascetic heritage: the five brahma-mantras, ash-observances, the Śaiva cosmos of principles

evidence.detail: The Mantramārga scriptures themselves place the Atimārga below the path of mantras in a graded hierarchy of religion (worldly, Vedic, spiritual, Atimārga, Mantramārga).

notes: U49 addition: the tradition's own ranking (see cpt:fivefold-hierarchy-of-religion).

what: The six-limbed yoga with prāṇāyāma, pratyāhāra, dhyāna, dhāraṇā and samādhi (Maitrī Upaniṣad: + tarka; Buddhist: + anusmṛti) — shared names, different order, signs and goal.

evidence.detail: Maitrī 6.18 (read locally): prāṇāyāma, pratyāhāra, dhyāna, dhāraṇā, tarka, samādhi; GST 18.138: pratyāhāra, dhyāna, prāṇāyāma, dhāraṇā, anusmṛti, samādhi — five names shared, the sixth differs, and the order differs.

notes: U49 addition: the local Maitrī text and the Amṛtanāda's list (which has the Maitrī's tarka).

what: A six-limbed yoga with reasoning (tarka) as one limb, in the Maitrī Upaniṣad and in the Śaiva Mantramārga.
era: Maitrī (c. last centuries BCE–early CE) → Śaiva tantras (c. 6th–9th c. CE)

evidence.detail: Both lists include tarka, absent from Patañjali's eight limbs and replaced by anusmṛti in the Buddhist six; the Mālinīvijayottara's six limbs include tarka (recalled) and the Mṛgendra adds recitation and examination (ūha) to the usual limbs.
A common older six-limbed yoga, rather than direct borrowing, is often proposed.

notes: New in U49; see cpt:six-limbed-yoga-across-families and cpt:tarka-as-limb.

what: Alchemical works and the ideal of the immortal perfected body ascribed to Buddhist siddhas, above all a Nāgārjuna held to be an alchemist (the Rasaratnākara).

evidence.detail: The Rasaratnākara is ascribed to Nāgārjuna; Tibetan and Chinese accounts credit Nāgārjuna with an elixir of long life; later tradition identifies the alchemist with the Madhyamaka master, which historians reject.
The Jain narrative literature (e.g. the Prabhāvakacarita) makes the alchemist Nāgārjuna a pupil of the Jain teacher Pādalipta — a third tradition's claim to the same figure (recalled).
Historians distinguish several Nāgārjunas (the Madhyamaka philosopher, the tantric siddha, the alchemist) and see a Buddhist strand in early rasa literature beside the Śaiva one.

notes: New in U49; low confidence. Restricted domain (metals/mercury): no recipes recorded.

what: Brahmanical deities received into the Buddhist tantric pantheon as protectors or subdued powers: Mahākāla, Gaṇapati (Vināyaka), Sarasvatī, the planets and the guardians of the directions; Maheśvara subdued and renamed in the maṇḍala.

evidence.detail: The Buddhist texts tell of the subjugation of Maheśvara and the worldly gods by Vajrapāṇi/Trailokyavijaya, who gives them places in the maṇḍala.
The same deity names (Mahākāla, Gaṇapati, Sarasvatī, the navagrahas, the lokapālas) in Buddhist sādhanas and maṇḍalas.
The same figures reach East Asian esoteric Buddhism: Daikokuten (Mahākāla), Benzaiten (Sarasvatī), Kangiten (the paired Vināyaka/Gaṇeśa) in Shingon and Tendai.
Historians describe this as the Buddhist appropriation of the Brahmanical pantheon; the Buddhist tradition describes it as conversion.

notes: New in U49; see cpt:taming-of-rival-deities.

what: The Buddha received into the Vaiṣṇava lists of Viṣṇu's descents — as a deluder of the enemies of the gods, and later (Jayadeva) as the compassionate critic of animal sacrifice.

evidence.detail: The Bhāgavata's avatāra list includes the Buddha; the Agni and Viṣṇu Purāṇas tell how Viṣṇu as Māyāmoha/the son of Śuddhodana led the daityas away from the Veda; Jayadeva praises the Buddha who condemned the slaughter of animals in sacrifice.
The Buddhist traditions do not accept the Buddha as an avatāra of Viṣṇu; the Vaiṣṇava accounts themselves differ on the purpose of the descent (dsp:buddha-avatara-purpose).

notes: New in U49.

what: Mutual shaping of Bön and Tibetan Buddhism beyond the Great Perfection: on the Bön side, monastic discipline, a canon arranged as Kangyur and Tengyur, scholastic curriculum and the nine-vehicle frame; on the Buddhist side, Tibetan rites of the local gods, ransom (glud) and fumigation (bsang) offerings, divination and the 'soul' (bla).
era: 8th c. onward; most visible from the 11th c.

evidence.detail: Each tradition claims priority: Bön holds that Tönpa Shenrab taught long before Śākyamuni and that Buddhists converted Bön texts; Buddhist polemics hold that Bön took over Buddhist scriptures by changing their terms.
Parallel technical vocabularies (e.g. bon for chos, g.yung drung for rdo rje) and shared ritual forms.
Historians describe 'eternal Bön' (g.yung drung bon) as formed in close interaction with Buddhism from the 11th c., while holding that pre-Buddhist Tibetan ritual survives in both.

notes: New in U49; complements brw:nyingma-bon-dzogchen (U45), which covers the Great Perfection only.

what: The Purāṇa genre — universal history, cosmology, genealogies and the lives of great beings — taken up by Jain authors as the lives of the sixty-three illustrious persons (Jinasena's Ādipurāṇa; Vimalasūri's Paumacariya), presented as the true account against the Brahmanical Purāṇas and epics.

evidence.detail: Jain Purāṇas and caritas follow the Purāṇic frame of creation, lineages and heroic lives with Jain content.

Vimalasūri's Paumacariya opens by rejecting the 'false' Rāma stories of the Brahmanical poets (monkeys as warriors, Rāvaṇa as a demon) and offers the Jina's true account; the Jain tradition does not regard its Purāṇas as borrowed.
Historians read the Jain Purāṇas as a Jain response to the Brahmanical genre.

notes: New in U49; content-level retellings are brw:jain-rama-narrative and brw:jain-krsna-narrative.

what: Pāṇini's system recast by Jain and Buddhist grammarians without the Vedic rules: the Jainendra (Devanandin/Pūjyapāda), Śākaṭāyana and Hemacandra's Siddhahemaśabdānuśāsana; the Buddhist Cāndra grammar.

evidence.detail: These grammars follow Pāṇini's rule-technique and ordering while omitting or rewriting the rules for Vedic forms and accent (recalled).
The Jain tradition treats its grammars as independent works for the Jain community; the Pāṇinian tradition regards grammar as a limb of the Veda.
Historians describe them as 'non-Vedic Pāṇinian' grammars.

notes: New in U49 (sources: src:jainendra-vyakarana, src:sakatayana-sabdanusasana, src:siddhahemasabdanusasana, src:candra-vyakarana). The Buddhist Cāndra grammar is the same kind of borrowing to lin:mahayana.

what: Kundakunda's teaching of the pure (niścaya) and conventional (vyavahāra) standpoints, with the conventional as the indispensable means of teaching the ultimate, compared with the Madhyamaka two truths.
era: c. 2nd–8th c. CE (Kundakunda's date is itself disputed)

evidence.detail: Samayasāra 8: as a non-Aryan cannot be taught except in a non-Aryan tongue, the ultimate cannot be taught without the conventional; MMK 24.10 (recalled): without relying on convention the ultimate is not taught. The foreign-language simile also occurs in Candrakīrti (recalled, low confidence).
The Jain tradition derives niścaya and vyavahāra from the canonical doctrine of standpoints (naya) and denies Buddhist or Vedāntic dependence.
Some historians see Madhyamaka or Vedāntic influence on Kundakunda; others hold the two-standpoint doctrine to be an internal Jain development.

notes: New in U49; see cpt:levels-of-truth-across-families.

what: Knowledge of a 'doctrine of no-self' (nairātmya-vāda) and of ochre-robed and skull-bearing ascetics in the Maitrī Upaniṣad, which warns against them, and its story of a deluding false knowledge created by Bṛhaspati for the asuras.
era: c. last centuries BCE – early centuries CE (scholarly date of the Maitrī)

evidence.detail: Maitrī 7.8 names the 'tricksters of the doctrine of no-self' and the kāpālins; 7.9 tells how Bṛhaspati, as Śukra, created a false knowledge to destroy the asuras (read locally).
Most historians take the nairātmya-vādins to be Buddhists and the passage as evidence of the Maitrī's post-Buddhist date; the Upaniṣadic tradition treats the text as śruti and does not date it.

notes: New in U49: an engagement (polemical reference), not an adoption. The deluding-doctrine motif recurs in the Purāṇic Māyāmoha story (cpt:taming-of-rival-deities).

what: A permanent, pure, blissful 'self' language for the buddha-nature present in all beings.
era: c. 3rd–5th c. CE (tathāgatagarbha sūtras and treatises)

evidence.detail: The Laṅkāvatāra itself raises the objection that the tathāgatagarbha teaching is like the non-Buddhists' doctrine of self (read locally, Vaidya p. 33).
The Mahāparinirvāṇa: 'self' means the tathāgatagarbha; the Ratnagotravibhāga: the perfections of purity, self, bliss and permanence.
The Buddhist tradition denies the likeness: the tathāgatagarbha is taught as a name for emptiness, by skilful means, to attract those who cling to a self.
Some scholars see Upaniṣadic influence on tathāgatagarbha language; others read it as an internal Buddhist development (the luminous mind).

notes: New in U49.

what: The charge, made by Tibetan critics, that the Jonang 'other-empty' ultimate — permanent and endowed with qualities — resembles the non-Buddhists' permanent self.

evidence.detail: Critics in other Tibetan schools argued that Dolpopa's permanent ultimate amounts to a non-Buddhist ātman; the Jonang answer that the ultimate is empty of the adventitious and is not a self of persons or things, and cite the Buddha-nature sūtras.
Historians treat the charge as polemical; no historical borrowing from Vedānta is claimed by either side.

notes: New in U49. Recorded because it is a tradition's own allegation of borrowing, with the accused tradition's denial.

what: The cosmography of Meru at the centre of Jambudvīpa, with Bhārata as the land of action, surrounded by continents and oceans — shared by Purāṇic, Jain and Buddhist (Abhidharma) texts with different geometries.
era: last centuries BCE – early centuries CE (scholarly)

evidence.detail: Meru, Jambudvīpa, Bhārata/Bharata, the salt ocean, the divine regions; the Jain and Purāṇic 'land of action' (karmabhūmi).
Each family presents its cosmography as revealed or seen by omniscience (the Jina's, the Buddha's, the seers').
A common Indian cosmographic stock, elaborated separately; direction not determinable.

notes: New in U49; the Buddhist variant is in cpt:meru-cosmography-across-families.

what: Epic narratives retold as past lives of the Buddha: the Rāma story in the Dasaratha Jātaka (Rāma as the bodhisatta, Sītā as his sister, no Rāvaṇa war) and the story of Vāsudeva/Kaṇha and his brothers in the Ghata Jātaka.

evidence.detail: Dasaratha Jātaka (Jā 461) and Ghata Jātaka (Jā 454) parallel the Rāma and Kṛṣṇa narratives (recalled).
The Buddhist tradition presents them as the Buddha's own past lives, told by him.
Whether the Jātaka Rāma story is older than Vālmīki's or dependent on an epic version is debated.

notes: New in U49; complements the Jain retellings (brw:jain-rama-narrative, brw:jain-krsna-narrative).

what: The syllable Oṃ at the head of Jain mantras (e.g. with hrīṃ and arhaṃ), explained as formed from the initials of the five supreme beings.

evidence.detail: Jain teachers derive oṃ from a (arhat) + a (aśarīra, the siddha) + ā (ācārya) + u (upādhyāya) + m (muni), making it a compressed homage to the five supreme beings (recalled from the Dravyasaṃgraha commentary tradition).
oṃ, hrīṃ and other seed syllables in Jain meditation on words (padastha).

notes: New in U49. The Jain tradition gives oṃ its own Jain meaning and does not present it as Vedic.

what: The syllable Oṃ opening Buddhist dhāraṇīs and mantras (oṃ maṇi padme hūṃ; oṃ āḥ hūṃ as body, speech and mind of the buddhas).

evidence.detail: oṃ as initial syllable of mantras; in the tantras oṃ āḥ hūṃ stand for the three vajras.
The Buddhist tantras give oṃ their own sense (the vajra-body) and do not present it as the Vedic praṇava.

notes: New in U49.

what: Doctrines of indivisible atoms (paramāṇu/aṇu) that combine into gross things — Vaiśeṣika, Jain (pudgala atoms and aggregates) and Buddhist Vaibhāṣika — and their critique by the Yogācāra.

evidence.detail: TS 5.25–28: matter is atoms and aggregates; aggregates arise by division, combination or both, the atom by division.
Vasubandhu's Viṃśatikā refutes the atoms of the Vaiśeṣikas and of the Kashmiri Vaibhāṣikas by name.
Each school derives its atomism from its own founder (Kaṇāda; the Jina) and none acknowledges borrowing.
Priority between Jain and Vaiśeṣika atomism is debated.

notes: New in U49.

what: Empirical healing practised in ascetic communities (the Buddhist Vinaya's medicines and physician Jīvaka), proposed as a source of classical Āyurveda.

evidence.detail: Āyurveda traces itself to Brahmā, Prajāpati, the Aśvins and Indra, from whom Bharadvāja received it — a divine, Vedic descent.
The Vinaya's chapter on medicines (the five basic medicines, oils, roots, decoctions) and the Jīvaka stories share materia medica with the Caraka tradition (recalled).
Some historians argue that heterodox ascetic medicine was later absorbed into Brahmanical Āyurveda; others see parallel development.

notes: New in U49; low confidence.

what: Brahmanical gods received as protectors of the Buddha's teaching in Sri Lankan Theravāda: the Buddha entrusts Laṅkā to Sakka, who entrusts it to the god Uppalavaṇṇa (later identified with Viṣṇu); shrines of Viṣṇu, Kataragama (Skanda) and others within monastery precincts.

evidence.detail: Mahāvaṃsa ch. 7 tells of the Buddha's charge to Sakka and Sakka's entrusting of Laṅkā to Uppalavaṇṇa (recalled).
The identification of Uppalavaṇṇa with Viṣṇu is later and debated.

notes: New in U49.

what: The language of the void (śūnya, the 'void person') and the identification of Jagannātha with the Buddha in the Oḍiā writings of the Pañcasakhā poets.

evidence.detail: The Pañcasakhā works speak of the formless void-person and some name Jagannātha as the Buddha form of Viṣṇu (recalled; low confidence).
Historians have proposed that Buddhist (Mahāyāna and siddha) ideas survived in Oḍiā Vaiṣṇavism ('hidden Buddhism'); others explain the language from Nāth and Vaiṣṇava sources.

notes: New in U49; low confidence, flagged in REPORT.md.

what: The Vedic identification of soma with the moon and with the drink of immortality (amṛta), internalized as the nectar dripping from the moon in the head that the haṭha yogin drinks or protects.

evidence.detail: soma, candra, amṛta: the haṭha texts speak of drinking the soma with the tongue turned upward and of the moon's nectar consumed by the sun.
Historians read the haṭha moon-nectar as an internalization of the Vedic soma complex; the haṭha texts do not cite the Veda for it.

notes: New in U49.
